where are you finding that the p2415q supports g-sync? i cant find that indicated anywhere, and it seems very unlikely given that the p series is dells professional line and is therefore focused on features that businesses care about, like built-in usb ports, height-adjustable stands, daisy chaining, etc.-- not gaming features like g-sync. but assuming you did buy g-sync displays, your ability to use it will depend on whether the gpu outputs exposed on the usb-c/tb3 port are wired to the intel gpu or nvidia gpu. if you want to find out, connect any display or tv to that port using something like a usb-c to dp/hdmi adapter or cable, then go to nvidia control panel > physx configuration. in there youll find a diagram showing which gpu controls each active display. if the display/tv you connected shows as being wired to the intel gpu, you wont be able to use g-sync regardless of which dock you get. g-sync requires that the display be directly controlled by the gpu and that the display be using displayport (or usb-c, which uses displayport for video traffic). g-sync does not run over hdmi, so that wont help you even if you find that the hdmi output is wired to the nvidia gpu -- which it might be in order to support vr headsets that use hdmi inputs, since vr also requires being wired directly to the nvidia gpu. but if you dont have a port that meets both of those earlier requirements (direct control by nvidia gpu and displayport/usb-c), then you cant run g-sync.

the answer to the gpu question is a bit more complicated on both sides. the d6000 uses displaylink. due to a windows limitation, displays attached via displaylink can only use gpu acceleration from the systems primary gpu. on a system with both an intel and nvidia gpu enabled, that will be the intel gpu. so youd never get the benefit of the nvidia gpu. but its worse than that. displaylink technology itself imposes some significant drawbacks for certain use cases, including and especially gaming. i wrote about those in detail in this thread, specifically the post marked as the answer. the bottom line is that displaylink performance is even worse than a display that was driven normally by the intel gpu, even if it didnt have access to the nvidia gpu. the wd19 family taps into the systems native gpu outputs available on usb-c or thunderbolt 3. as a result, none of the penalties of displaylink apply, and displays attached to that dock will have access to the nvidia gpu just as if you attached a display directly to the system. however, on most display outputs of systems -- and all usb-c/t3 outputs that ive seen on dell systems thus far -- the intel gpu still has direct control of the output itself. that means that the nvidia gpu when needed steps in as a render-only device to do the heavy lifting and then passes completed video frames to the intel gpu for output to the attached displays. this technology is called nvidia optimus. the vast majority of laptops are set up this way because by preventing the nvidia gpu from having direct control of display outputs, it can be completely disabled when its not needed, which saves battery life. if the nvidia gpu had direct control of outputs, then it would need to be active whenever a display was attached, even if nothing graphics-intensive was going on. the catch is that there are certain technologies that the intel gpu doesnt support passing through and/or that nvidia gpus can only use if they have direct control of the display output. these include vr, g-sync, adaptive v-sync, stereoscopic 3d, and a few others. however, once again that isnt a limitation of the dock. its simply an aspect of the system design. certain systems have at least some display outputs directly wired to the nvidia gpu instead specifically to make it possible to use those technologies i just listed, but i dont know if the 5590 is set up that way, and once again on every dell system ive seen, the usb-c/tb3 ports are always wired to the intel gpu (except the precision 7000 series models where a bios option allows you to choose which gpu has control of the display outputs).

a few things to clarify right away here: if your display supports displayport, id recommend a usb-c to displayport cable/adapter instead. usb-c uses displayport for video output anyway, so usb-c to hdmi adapters/cables have to incorporate an active converter chip to switch that signal to hdmi. thats just one more thing to pay for and potentially cause problems, so if you dont actually need it, then avoid it. your laptop likely does not support being charged over usb-c/tb3, so i would not expect the wd19tb to charge your system. the wd19tb supports providing up to 130w over usb-c/tb3, but thats only possible when the system also does. dell systems like the s 15 and some precision systems support that, but every post ive seen from people using inspiron gaming systems indicates that they do not support it, even when the system is designed for a 130w power source. but some inspiron gaming systems use 180w power sources, and in that case even if 130w charging was supported, youd see reduced performance due to using an undersized power source. so the wd19tb can still be useful if you want to connect high end display setups like dual 4 mil 60 hz through a single cable, but i would not expect it to charge your system. absolutely do not get the dell d6000. it uses indirect display technology called displaylink (not to be confused with displayport), and that introduces some drawbacks that can be significant in many use cases, especially gaming. i wrote about those in the post marked as the answer in this thread. in terms of whether you can use the monitors with the nvidia rtx gpu, as long as you do not use something like the d6000, you will at least be able to use the nvidia gpu through nvidia optimus. that will allow the nvidia gpu to handle rendering, so youll get high performance. this is how most dual gpu laptops work. the outputs are actually wired to the intel gpu, but the nvidia gpu can operate as a render-only device when needed and pass video through the intel gpu. however, in that setup, certain features will not be available, such as g-sync, adaptive v-sync, vr, and a few others. those require the nvidia gpu to have direct control of the display output, which isnt a very common design. since this is an inspiron gaming system, you might actually find that the hdmi output is wired to the nvidia gpu since dell did that on some systems in order to allow using hdmi-based vr headsets. but the usb-c/tb3 output might be wired to the intel gpu. if you want to check, connect a display to the output you want to test, then go to nvidia control panel > physx configuration. in there, youll find a diagram showing which active displays are wired to which gpu. then repeat this test for any other display output you want to test.

theres no industry-wide standard for an external power button. its something that vendors all implement via their own proprietary solutions, which require firmware-level support within the system to allow itself to be controlled from that external button. the d6000 is marketed as a universal dock, including non-dell systems, and since theres no way to have a universal external power button, it doesnt have one. the wd19, wd19tb etc. are not billed as universal docks. however, even within dells own system lineup, it seems that dell hasnt implemented support for an external power button across all product lines. the latitude, precision, and s systems have them because the wd family docks are explicitly marketed as being fully compatible with those systems. but support for this on inspiron, vostro, and alienware systems seems much less consistent. incidentally, there are other features of the wd family docks that also require firmware support from the system, including mac address passthrough, possibly wake on lan, and i believe even the ability to update the firmware of the dock, since that involves a system reboot and an update that occurs during boot time, sort of like a bios update. so you might find that you cant update the docks firmware from certain dell systems either.

i know it would work with them in the sense that you can send a picture to them, but my understanding is that you wouldnt be able to use the actual g-sync feature with them. the dell d6000 uses displaylink (not to be confused with displayport), and due to a windows limitation, that means that on systems with both intel and nvidia gpus active, you cant even use the nvidia gpus graphical acceleration horsepower, because displaylink will only allow you to use the primary gpu, which in dual gpu systems will be the intel gpu. and g-sync requires not only that the nvidia gpu be used, but that it have direct control of the display output connector. on most laptops, the nvidia gpu doesnt have direct control of any outputs and instead works through nvidia optimus as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the intel gpu, which is directly connected to the display outputs. but displaylink in particular is an indirect display technology that involves compressing rendered video and transmitting it as regular usb data. thats how the d6000 and other displaylink-based adapters and docks can support plugging into a system over usb-a, which has no native video output support. so in that case, neither of the systems gpus would have direct control of the display output connector. if youre claiming that the d6000 supports g-sync displays and that g-sync can actually be enabled for such displays when connected through the d6000, what is your source for that?

hey everyone, i found a solution! i know this is years later, but i have the g5 15 5590 (i7-9750h, nvidia rtx 2060), and ive been struggling with high temps too, and not being able to undervolt due to bios updates... well, heres the solution: power options (built into windows 10 & 11). when you go to your power options, and hit advanced settings, there is an option for processor power management. under this, my laptop was set to have the min and max processor state at 100% when plugged in. i changed the max to 90%, and min to 10%, and my temps immediately dropped. playing satisfactory, cpu was at 95-100c, and changing max processor state to 90% dropped cpu temps to 70c max. yes, a 30 degree c drop! even better, framerate was unaffected (at least in my sample size of 1 game). i dont know if this is the same thing as undervolting, but the end result is lower temps and no fps loss in game. idle temps for my cpu went from 60-70c at 100% to 45-47c at 90%. if anyone is still rocking the g5 15 5590 (or any laptop with temp issues for that matter) this option built right into windows works great!(tested on my laptop with windows 11 and desktop with windows 10) in windows 11, hit the start button, type power plan and hit edit power plan, then click change advanced power settings. in this new window, you can find and edit the processor power management.

attached to it anyway to maintain an appropriately sized power source. a thunderbolt 3 dock would have access to enough display bandwidth to run your proposed display setup because it can run dual 4 the exception of the precision 7000 series that allow customization here, all dell and alienware systems have their usb-c/tb3 video output wired to the intel gpu, not the nvidia gpu. the nvidia gpu operates only indirectly via a technology called nvidia optimus. but since the intel gpu has direct control of the display output, i dont know how well it runs 144 hz. in addition, nvidia gpus using optimus cannot use adaptive v-sync or g-sync. your only options are v-sync off or v-sync on, and that creates a bit of dilemma when dealing with a high refresh rate display. if you use v-sync off, then you can see frame tearing, which is precisely what v-sync is meant to eliminate. but if you turn v-sync on, then when using a 144 hz display, youll need to make sure your system can maintain a stable 144 fps, because whenever it cant, youll see stuttering or judder, which can be just as distracting and annoying as frame tearing. a mid-range gaming laptop is unlikely to be able to sustain 144 fps in modern games, at least not without turning the detail way down. this dilemma is precisely why g-sync was created, since it eliminates frame tearing while also allowing the displays refresh rate to change based on the frame rate the gpu can handle at any given time, which means you also eliminate stutter/judder -- but again that probably wont be available here. but in terms of docks, the most dell systems have their usb-c/tb3 video outputs wired to the intel gpu. only a small number of systems have them wired to the nvidia gpu or offer a bios option to allow you to choose which gpu controls the outputs. the latter capability is something that i’ve only seen within dell systems on the precision 7000 series systems, and more recently on the s 17 9700/precision 5750 but only when ordered with an rtx gpu. it’s likely that your system has that output wired to the intel gpu without the necessary bios option to change it because it doesn’t have the necessary motherboard design to offer that type of flexibility. and the intel gpus built into core 9th gen cpus only supports displayport 1.2/hbr2, which is only enough bandwidth for 4 mil 60 hz. a tb3 connection can carry dual dp 1.2 source interfaces from the gpu, but intel gpus do not support aggregating multiple interfaces to drive a single display. so tb3 could allow you to drive dual 4 mil 60 hz, but not single 4 mil 120 hz even though those two setups require the same total bandwidth. disabling optimus in your case would simply disable the nvidia gpu. it would not remove the intel gpu from the video path, since that isn’t possible on your system’s design, at least for its usb-c/tb3 port. all that said, if nvidia control panel indicates that the mdp output is directly controlled by the nvidia gpu, then that would be the right choice, since that output might support dp 1.4/hbr3. if the port stops working when playing games and gets overheated, it sounds like you have a hardware issue though.

while im not familiar with your particular model i suspect that it has a lithium polymer battery like my vostro 5502. lipo batteries do not like to be deep discharged. i had two deep discharge events (down to near 0% charge) with my vostro and each time the capacity decreased slightly. its now down to 92.2%. the solution is to not let the battery drop to below 30% capacity. when you hit 30%, plug it in. another problem with deep discharging is that the battery will start to puff. flammable hydrogen gas will start to build up inside the battery casing and the battery will start to grow larger. this is why you hear about people having touchpad and keyboard problems. the battery expands and starts pressing on things it should not be pressing on. yes, i said flammable. look up lipo fire on youtube. ive been playing with lipo batteries since 2009 for model airplane use. i learned early on not to deep discharge lipos. i have some in service that are over 7 years old and they still hold a good charge. i have gotten good at timing flights and tend to land with the batteries at 50% capacity. another top tip is if you intend to let your laptop sit unused for more than two weeks perform a storage charge. a storage charge is simply charge or discharge the battery to 60%. it will then be safe to leave the laptop unused for months. never leave a lipo battery unused for long periods of time fully charged, it will ultimately reduce the fully charged capacity. all of my fancy lipo chargers have a storage charge function to automate this process. this function will either charge of discharge the battery to 60% automatically. in summary, do not discharge your laptop below 30% and you should no longer see the decrease in fully charged capacity assuming that your battery is not already too far gone. dell should be telling us about this but they are in the business of selling replacement laptops and laptop batteries.

you can install drivers downloaded directly from nvidia onto your laptop, but enabling stereoscopic 3d requires that the nvidia gpu be directly wired to the display you want to use, and that might not be the case in your system. in most laptops with both integrated (intel) and discrete gpus, the built-in display is still wired to the integrated gpu, and in many cases most or even all external display outputs are also wired to the integrated gpu. in those cases, when the discrete gpus extra performance is needed, it acts as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the integrated gpu for output to the display(s). for nvidia, this technology is called optimus. the benefit of this design is that when the discrete gpus performance is not needed, it can be completely disabled, which saves battery life, but the downside is that certain technologies that the intel gpu does not support passing through and/or that are proprietary to nvidia and therefore always require the nvidia gpu to have direct control of the display output arent available. those technologies include stereoscopic 3d, g-sync, vr, and some others. in nvidia control panel, if you check either the physx or multi-display area, i believe one of those areas shows a diagram indicating which displays are wired to which gpu. that might be useful.

minidp doesnt supply any meaningful amount of power. the display runs from its own power source. my guess as to whats happening here is that the gpu outputs driving the usb-c/tb3 port on that system are wired to the intel gpu and the minidp port built into the system is wired to the nvidia gpu. you can confirm this if you go to nvidia control panel and select physx configuration, which will show you which displays are being directly driven by which gpu. see how your display shows up when connected via both methods. the nvidia gpu can work even on displays connected to the dock through a technology called nvidia optimus, which allows the nvidia gpu to act as a render-only device that passes completed video frames to the intel gpu for output to the display(s) that its directly driving (which likely includes the systems built-in display, fyi), but its possible that the intel gpu is trying to decode that 4 mil video itself and/or that the nvidia gpu is doing it and optimus isnt working as it should. what application are you trying to use? does it allow you to choose different video render engines? in any case, no a higher wattage adapter wont do anything because the dock isnt supply power through its mini-displayport output or doing any other sort of graphics work. its just passing a displayport signal from the laptop out of that port. on a side note, i really recommend against using 2 mil as a resolution term because so many people use it incorrectly to refer to 2560x1440 resolution, which creates confusion, and sometimes the difference can matter for technical reasons.2 mil resolution is technically a film resolution of 2048x1080, but when used to refer to consumer resolutions, it actually refers to the nearest and slightly lower consumer equivalent, which is 1920x1080, aka full hd or 1080p -- because 1920 is very close to 2000, i. e.2 mil, horizontal pixels. similarly,4 mil is also technically a film resolution of 4096x2160 pixels, but when used in the consumer world refers to the slightly lower resolution of 3840x2160, aka ultra hd or 2160p. if you actually meant to refer to 2560x1440, that resolution is rightfully called 1440p or qhd (or i guess you could call it 2.5 mil, but nobody does). using either of those terms would make it much clearer to everyone what youre talking about. the reason it can matter is because the bandwidth difference between 1080p and 1440p displays affects available display configurations in certain setups. for example, if someone had a wd15 dock and said,why cant i run dual 2 mil displays?, if they were trying to use dual 1080p displays, that should be possible -- but if they were trying to run dual 1440p displays, that would not be possible because the wd15 doesnt have enough bandwidth for that. but if they say 2 mil meaning one thing and someone else assumes they mean the other, you could end up going down the wrong path on troubleshooting for a while.

g-sync only works over displayport (and usb-c, which uses displayport signaling for video), but it also requires that the display output be wired directly to the nvidia gpu. many laptops have most or all outputs wired to the intel gpu, with the nvidia gpu operating as a render-only device through a technology called nvidia optimus. that has battery life advantages since it allows the nvidia gpu to be completely disabled when its horsepower isnt needed, but it prevents g-sync from being used (as well as vr, adaptive v-sync, stereoscopic 3d, and some other technologies). so before you buy your display, check whether either the usb-c or mini-displayport output is wired to the nvidia gpu. to do that, connect a display to the output, then go to nvidia control panel and open the physx configuration section, which will include a diagram showing which gpu controls each active display. if the display you connected as a test shows as being wired to the intel gpu, you wont be able to use g-sync through that output. to my knowledge, all current dell systems have their usb-c/tb3 ports wired to the intel gpu, except precision 7000 series systems that have a bios option allowing you to choose which gpu controls the display outputs -- but that capability doesnt seem to be implemented elsewhere. the mini-displayport output is your best bet here, because some alienware and inspiron gaming systems do have at least one display output wired to the discrete gpu specifically to support technologies like vr, g-sync, etc. in terms of cables, im pretty sure 1440p 165 hz will run over a regular displayport 1.2 interface, in which case you wouldnt need anything special because displayport 1.2 has been around for a long time, so youd need a truly ancient displayport cable for it not to support at least 1.2.

ok first of all, ahci and uefi are not opposites. theyre completely different things that are configured in completely different sections of the bios setup. uefi is a boot type, and the other boot type option is legacy (aka bios). ahci is a storage interface operation mode, and the other option there is raid. despite the sata operation setting name, it also affects how the system treats nvme ssds. but the point is that you can can have a system that boots in uefi mode and runs its storage interface in ahci mode -- or a system that boots in uefi mode and runs its storage interface in raid mode, which is the factory default configuration. the reason youre having an issue is that as you should have been warned when you tried to change the raid setting to ahci, that setting isnt meant to be changed on an installed os. its designed to be changed before you reinstall an os. the reason is that if windows is installed while the system is in raid mode, then it will configure itself to load the intel rapid storage driver at boot in order to see the storage device. if you then reconfigure the system to run in ahci mode, then windows wont be configured to load the correct driver at boot anymore, so it will fail. in order to reduce boot time, there are certain devices and drivers where windows does not dynamically adjust based on the installed hardware and its configuration. instead, it just stores assumptions about how the hardware will be configured, so if you change the hardware configuration, then those assumptions are invalid and windows doesnt start. the same would occur if you had installed windows while in ahci mode and later decided to switch to raid. there are some manual hoops you can jump through in order to switch an existing windows installation over to ahci mode. they involve booting in safe mode at some point and possibly some other tasks. i havent looked into them in detail. but if you were to perform multiple benchmarks in both raid mode and ahci mode, i doubt youd see much of a consistent performance difference, if any at all. so if youre not all that techy, you might want to just leave this one alone.
